hook: China's best-loved poet, of wine, mountains and the moon.

pages.x: Li Bai grew up in Sichuan, in western China; he may have been born in Central Asia. As a young man he practised swordsmanship, lived with hermits in the mountains and, he boasted, fought several duels. At 24 he set off down the Yangtze to see the world.

His poems made him so famous that in 742 Emperor Xuanzong called him to the capital, Chang'an. Legend says the emperor stirred his soup for him, and that Li Bai, drunk, made a powerful palace official pull off his boots. He did not last long at court.

His most famous poem is learned by every Chinese child: "Before my bed the moonlight glows, like frost upon the ground. I lift my head to see the moon, then bow it, thinking of home." About 1,000 of his poems survive, on wine, friendship, mountains and the moon.

In another poem he drinks alone among the flowers, so he invites the moon and his own shadow to join him, making a party of three. A friend wrote that he could dash off a hundred poems for one jug of wine.

In 755 a great rebellion tore China apart. Li Bai joined a prince who turned out to be a rebel, and was sentenced to exile in the far south-west. He was pardoned on the way and spent his last years wandering the Yangtze.
He died in 762. A famous legend says he drowned one night when, drunk in a boat on the Yangtze, he leaned out to hug the reflection of the moon in the water.
Li Bai and his friend Du Fu are the giants of Chinese poetry. Translated by Ezra Pound and set to music by Gustav Mahler, his poems shaped how the whole world imagines Chinese verse.
